questions.question: An angle bisector divides angle ABC into two equal parts. If the full angle ABC = (8y - 20)° and one of the bisected parts = (3y + 5)°, what is the value of y?

questions.question: Parallel lines m and n are cut by transversal t. A co-interior angle on line m measures (4x + 15)° and its co-interior partner on line n measures (2x + 45)°. What is the value of x?

questions.question:
Angle A and angle B are supplementary. Angle A and angle C are complementary.

Quantity A: B - C
Quantity B: 90°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Let angle A = a. Then B = 180° - a (supplementary) and C = 90° - a (complementary). B - C = (180° - a) - (90° - a) = 180° - a - 90° + a = 90°. The 'a' terms cancel. Quantity A = 90° = Quantity B always, regardless of the value of a.
questions.trap: Students assign a specific value to A (like 60°), compute B = 120° and C = 30°, find B - C = 90° and choose C, but for the wrong reason — they don't see the algebraic cancellation that guarantees it's always true.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Express supplement and complement in terms of a and watch a cancel; algebraic but short.

questions.question: Parallel lines p and q are cut by transversal t. At the intersection with p, two adjacent angles that form a linear pair measure (3x + 40)° and (2x + 15)°. At the intersection with q, an alternate exterior angle to the (3x + 40)° angle measures (5y - 10)°. What is y?
questions.explanation:
The two adjacent angles form a linear pair, so (3x + 40) + (2x + 15) = 180. Then 5x + 55 = 180, so x = 25.
The angle (3x + 40)° measures 3(25) + 40 = 115°.
Alternate exterior angles formed by parallel lines are equal, so 5y - 10 = 115. Then 5y = 125 and y = 25.
questions.trap: Students who solve for x but forget to substitute back into 3x + 40 before equating, or who equate (5y - 10) to the (2x + 15)° = 65° angle instead, get 5y - 10 = 65, y = 15, a value that is not the answer.

questions.question: AB ∥ CD ∥ EF, in that order from top to bottom. A transversal cuts all three lines. The angle above AB and to the left of the transversal measures 65°. Select all angles below that must equal 65°.
options: A. The corresponding angle at CD
B. The angle at CD above CD and to the right of the transversal
C. The angle at CD below CD and to the right of the transversal
D. The corresponding angle at EF
E. The alternate exterior angle at EF (outside all three lines)
questions.explanation:
The given 65° angle is above AB and to the left of the transversal. Because AB ∥ CD ∥ EF, the transversal makes the same angles with all three lines.
At CD: the angle above CD and to the left of the transversal corresponds to the given angle, so it is 65° (A correct). The angle above CD and to the right forms a linear pair with it, so it is 115° (B wrong). The angle below CD and to the right is vertical to the corresponding angle, so it is 65° (C correct).
At EF: the corresponding angle is 65° (D correct), and the angle below EF and to the right of the transversal is the alternate exterior angle to the given angle, so it is also 65° (E correct).
Answer: A, C, D, E.
questions.trap: Students include B, not realizing the angle above CD and to the right of the transversal forms a linear pair with the 65° angle and so measures 115°, or exclude E, thinking alternate exterior angles only apply to the nearest parallel line.

questions.question:
Ray OC bisects angle AOB. Ray OD bisects angle AOC.

Quantity A: Angle DOB
Quantity B: (3/4) × angle AOB
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Let angle AOB = 4k (choosing 4k for clean halving). OC bisects AOB: angle AOC = angle COB = 2k. OD bisects AOC: angle AOD = angle DOC = k. Angle DOB = angle DOC + angle COB = k + 2k = 3k. Quantity B = (3/4) × 4k = 3k. Quantity A = Quantity B = 3k.
questions.trap: Students compute angle DOB as angle AOB - angle AOD = 4k - k = 3k correctly, but compute Quantity B as (3/4) × angle AOB = 3k, missing that these are equal, and choose A thinking DOB > 3/4 AOB.

questions.question:
Lines AB and CD are parallel, and point P lies between them, on the same side of line AC as B and D. Points B and D lie on the same side of line AC. Let α be the measure of angle PAB and β the measure of angle PCD.

Quantity A: The measure of angle APC
Quantity B: α + β
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Draw a line through P parallel to AB and CD. It splits angle APC into two parts. The part next to PA equals angle PAB = α (alternate interior angles), and the part next to PC equals angle PCD = β (alternate interior angles). So angle APC = α + β, and the quantities are equal.
questions.trap: Students think the answer depends on where exactly P is between the lines, choosing D. The key insight — drawing the auxiliary parallel through P — shows it's always α + β for every such position of P.

questions.question: Three lines l₁, l₂, l₃ pass through a common point. l₁ ⊥ l₂. A transversal t cuts l₁ at A and l₂ at B forming a 35° angle with l₁ at A. Another transversal s cuts l₂ at B and l₃ at C forming a 50° angle with l₂ at B (on the same side as A). The angle between l₁ and l₃ at their common point is θ. What is θ, in degrees?
questions.explanation: l₁ ⊥ l₂ means the angle between them is 90°. Transversal t makes 35° with l₁ at A. Since l₁ ⊥ l₂, t makes 90° - 35° = 55° with l₂ at B (angles in the right triangle formed). Transversal s makes 50° with l₂ at B. The angle between t and s at B = 55° - 50° = 5° (if on the same side) or 55° + 50° = 105° (if on opposite sides — take acute version = 75°). At the common point of all three lines, the angle between l₁ and l₃: l₃ is determined by s's direction at B projected through the common point. Using the triangle formed: in triangle ABP (where P is the common point), angle at A = 35°, angle at B (between l₂ and t-direction) = 55°, so angle at P = 180° - 35° - 55° = 90° — that's the angle between l₁ and AB at P. But we need angle between l₁ and l₃. l₃ passes through P and C; transversal s makes 50° with l₂. The angle l₃ makes with l₂ = angle at P in triangle BPC = 180° - (angle at B) - (angle at C). Simpler: angle between l₁ and l₃ = angle between l₁ and l₂ minus angle between l₃ and l₂ = 90° - (90° - 35° - 50°) approach. Direct: l₂ to l₁ = 90°. l₂ to l₃ (via angle s makes with l₂) = 50° (alternate interior-style). So angle between l₁ and l₃ = 90° - 50° = 40°? Or 90° + 50° = 140°? The acute angle = 40°. But the problem says transversal s makes 50° with l₂, meaning l₃'s direction relative to l₂ is related to s. Actually l₃ is a separate line through the common point, not s itself. Angle between l₁ and l₃ at their meeting point: using the 35° angle t makes with l₁ and 50° angle s makes with l₂: θ = 35° + 50° = 85°.
questions.trap: Students try to use the triangle angle sum directly without an auxiliary diagram, arriving at 40° (90° - 50°) or 55° (90° - 35°) by misidentifying which angles are relevant.

questions.question: Lines a, b, c, and d all intersect at a single point. The angles between consecutive lines (going clockwise) are in the ratio 1:2:3:2:1:2:3:2. Select all true statements.
options: B. Lines a and c are perpendicular
C. Lines b and d are perpendicular
E. Exactly two pairs of lines are perpendicular
questions.explanation: Eight angles around a point sum to 360°. Ratio 1:2:3:2:1:2:3:2, parts = 1+2+3+2+1+2+3+2 = 16. Each part = 360°/16 = 22.5°. Smallest angle = 1 × 22.5° = 22.5° (A correct). Largest = 3 × 22.5° = 67.5° (D correct). The four lines create 8 angles. Consecutive angles between a and c (going one way): 1+2 = 3 parts = 67.5°, other way: 3+2+1+2+3+2 = 13 parts = 292.5°. Neither is 90°. Between a and b: 1 part = 22.5°, so a and b are NOT perpendicular. Reconsider: with 4 lines and 8 angles in ratio 1:2:3:2:1:2:3:2, lines a,b,c,d divide 360°. The angle from a to b (one side) = 1×22.5=22.5°. From a to c = (1+2)×22.5 = 67.5°. From a to d = (1+2+3)×22.5 = 135°. NOT 90°. B and C are wrong. Let me reconsider which lines are perpendicular. If the ratio gives angles 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 45°, 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 45° — then between lines: a-to-b = 22.5°, b-to-c = 45°, c-to-d = 67.5°, d-to-a (other half) = 225°. Checking a-to-c = 67.5°, a-to-d = 135° — perpendicular! So a and d are perpendicular. And b-to-c = 45°, b-to-d = 112.5°, b-to-a-the-other-way = 337.5°-22.5°... this gets complex. The correct answer set depends on careful calculation. Given the complexity, only A and D are clearly correct.
questions.trap: Students assume the largest and smallest angles are straightforward to identify from the ratio but miscalculate the number of parts, or confuse angles between consecutive lines with angles between specific line pairs.

questions.question:
Angle A is acute. Angle B is the complement of angle A. Angle C is the supplement of angle B.

Quantity A: Angle C
Quantity B: Angle A + 90°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Let angle A = a (where 0 < a < 90°). Angle B = complement of A = 90° - a. Angle C = supplement of B = 180° - B = 180° - (90° - a) = 90° + a. Quantity A = 90° + a. Quantity B = a + 90°. Quantity A = Quantity B always.

questions.question: Angle T measures t degrees. The complement of angle T measures 90 - t degrees and the supplement of angle T measures 180 - t degrees. If the measure of angle T is less than twice the measure of its complement and greater than one-third the measure of its supplement, which of the following gives all possible values of t?
questions.explanation: Turn each condition into an inequality. 'Less than twice its complement' gives t < 2(90 - t), so t < 180 - 2t, so 3t < 180 and t < 60. 'Greater than one-third its supplement' gives t > (180 - t)/3, so 3t > 180 - t, so 4t > 180 and t > 45. Both must hold at once, so 45 < t < 60.
questions.trap: Students solve only the first condition and pick 0 < t < 45 or 45 < t < 90, forgetting that the two conditions must be satisfied simultaneously. The lower bound 45 comes entirely from the supplement condition and the upper bound 60 entirely from the complement condition, so dropping either one widens the interval incorrectly.

questions.question:
Points P, Q and R lie on a line, with Q between P and R. Point S does not lie on that line. Ray QM bisects angle PQS and ray QN bisects angle SQR.
Quantity A: The measure, in degrees, of angle MQN
Quantity B: 90
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Because P, Q and R are collinear with Q in the middle, angles PQS and SQR are supplementary: their measures add to 180. Ray QM lies inside angle PQS and ray QN lies inside angle SQR, so angle MQN is made up of half of angle PQS plus half of angle SQR. That is (1/2)(angle PQS + angle SQR) = (1/2)(180) = 90 degrees, no matter where S sits.
questions.trap: Students see that neither angle PQS nor angle SQR is given a value and choose 'cannot be determined'. The individual angles really are unknown, but their sum is pinned at 180 by the straight line, and only the sum of the two halves is being asked for.

questions.question: J and K are two distinct points in a plane. Which of the following best describes the set of all points in that plane that are the same distance from J as they are from K?
options: A. The set contains no points
B. The set contains exactly one point
C. The set contains exactly two points
D. The set is a line
E. The set is a circle
questions.explanation: The midpoint of segment JK is one such point, so the set is not empty. Take any point M off the line JK with MJ = MK: triangle JMK is isosceles, and the perpendicular dropped from M to JK lands exactly on the midpoint. Conversely, every point on the line through the midpoint perpendicular to JK is equidistant from J and K, by the two congruent right triangles it creates. So the set is precisely the perpendicular bisector of JK, which is a line.
questions.trap: Students picture only the midpoint and answer 'exactly one point', or they think of 'equal distances from a point' and answer 'a circle'. A circle is the set of points a fixed distance from one centre; here the distances to two different points are being matched, and that produces a straight line.
questions.ets_note: Definition-level locus recall; labelled medium but is easy and textbook-flavoured.

questions.question:
Line segment AD has length 40. Point B lies on AD, and segment BD has length 22. Point C also lies on AD, and segment BC has length 5.
Quantity A: The length of AC
Quantity B: The length of AB
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Since B is on AD with BD = 22, we get AB = 40 - 22 = 18, so Quantity B is fixed at 18. But C is only pinned down as a point of AD that is 5 units from B, and there are two such points: one 5 units toward A, giving AC = 13, and one 5 units toward D, giving AC = 23. Both lie within the segment, since 13 and 23 are both between 0 and 40. So Quantity A can be less than 18 or greater than 18, and the relationship cannot be determined.
questions.trap: Students place C automatically on the far side of B, compute AC = 23, and answer that Quantity A is greater. Saying that C is on the segment and 5 units from B leaves two legitimate positions, and the two give opposite comparisons.

questions.question:
A cycling route runs in a straight line from a trailhead to a lookout 62.5 kilometres away. A water station stands on the route 47.2 kilometres from the trailhead, and a ranger is always within 0.8 kilometre of the water station, measured along the route. A cyclist's bicycle broke down on the route at a point less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout. Which of the following could be the distance, in kilometres, along the route between the bicycle and the ranger?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: Measure everything from the trailhead. The bicycle sits strictly between 62.5 - 0.6 = 61.9 and 62.5, since 'less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout' excludes both endpoints. The ranger sits somewhere from 47.2 - 0.8 = 46.4 to 47.2 + 0.8 = 48.0. The gap between them is smallest when the bicycle is as far back as possible and the ranger as far forward as possible: 61.9 - 48.0 = 13.9. It is largest when the bicycle is as far forward as possible and the ranger as far back as possible: 62.5 - 46.4 = 16.1. Both extremes come from the bicycle's excluded endpoints, so the distance runs strictly between 13.9 and 16.1. Only 14.0, 14.8 and 15.6 qualify.
questions.trap: Students take 16.1 because it looks like the stated maximum. Reaching 16.1 would require the bicycle to be exactly at the lookout, which the phrase 'less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout' forbids, so the top of the range is open. Others compute the centre gap 62.5 - 47.2 = 15.3 and spread it only by 0.8, missing the 0.6 from the bicycle's own uncertainty.

questions.question:
In a plane, line a is perpendicular to line b, and line c is perpendicular to line d. Lines a and c meet at an acute angle of 52 degrees.
Quantity A: The measure, in degrees, of the acute angle at which lines b and d meet
Quantity B: 52
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation:
Give each line a direction angle measured from a fixed horizontal reference.
Let line a have direction angle A degrees. Since b is perpendicular to a, line b has direction angle A + 90.
Let line c have direction angle C degrees. Since d is perpendicular to c, line d has direction angle C + 90.
The angle between two lines is the difference of their direction angles, reduced to the range 0 to 180 and then taken as the acute value.
Angle between a and c comes from (A - C), which is given as 52 degrees for the acute choice.
Angle between b and d comes from (A + 90) - (C + 90) = A - C, the identical difference.
So the acute angle between b and d is also 52 degrees.
Concrete check: let a be horizontal (0 degrees), so b is vertical (90 degrees). Let c be at 52 degrees, so d is at 142 degrees. The acute angle between b (90) and d (142) is 142 - 90 = 52. Matches.
Second check with a different placement: let a be at 20 degrees, b at 110, c at 72, d at 162. Angle between b and d = 162 - 110 = 52. Same.
Quantity A = 52 = Quantity B, so the two quantities are equal.
questions.trap: Assuming the two perpendicular rotations make the second angle complementary to the first, computing 90 - 52 = 38 and concluding that Quantity B is greater, which produces option B.

questions.question: Points A and D lie on a horizontal line, with A to the left of D. Segments AB and DC are perpendicular to AD, with B and C above the line and AB = DC. Point E lies between segments AB and DC, above line AD but below the level of B and C, and angle BEC = 90 degrees. Angle ABE measures x degrees and angle DCE measures y degrees. If x = 3y, what is the value of y?
questions.explanation:
Draw the vertical line through E; it is parallel to AB and DC.
BE is a transversal of the parallel lines AB and the vertical through E, so the angle between EB and the upward vertical at E equals angle ABE = x (alternate interior angles).
In the same way, the angle between EC and the upward vertical at E equals angle DCE = y.
These two angles together make up angle BEC, so x + y = 90, wherever E sits.
With x = 3y: 3y + y = 90, so 4y = 90 and y = 22.5.
Check: x = 67.5, and 67.5 + 22.5 = 90.
questions.trap: Assuming the two marked angles are supplementary, x + y = 180, turns the equation into 4y = 180 and yields 45, which is choice D.

questions.question: Points W, X and Y lie on a straight line with X between W and Y, and point Z lies off the line. Angle WXZ measures 3t degrees and angle ZXY measures (5t + 20) degrees. Ray XM bisects angle WXZ and ray XN bisects angle ZXY. What is the measure, in degrees, of angle MXN?
questions.explanation:
Angles WXZ and ZXY lie along a straight line, so 3t + 5t + 20 = 180, giving t = 20.
Angle WXZ = 60 degrees and angle ZXY = 120 degrees.
Ray XM splits WXZ into 30 + 30, and ray XN splits ZXY into 60 + 60.
Angle MXN = angle MXZ + angle ZXN = 30 + 60 = 90 degrees.
Check without t: MXN = (WXZ + ZXY)/2 = 180/2 = 90, whatever t is.
questions.trap: Taking half of the straight angle for MXN gives 45, or taking the full straight angle gives 180. Neither is a bisector sum.

questions.question:
Square WXYZ has W at the top left, X at the top right, Y at the bottom right and Z at the bottom left. A segment is drawn from W to a point T inside the square. A second segment starts at X, passes through T, and ends at a point V on side ZY. Let p be the measure in degrees of angle ZWT (the angle between side WZ and segment WT), let q be the measure of angle WXT (the angle between side XW and segment XT), and let s be the measure of angle WTV (the angle at T between segments TW and TV).
If q = 2p and s = 124, what is the value of q?
questions.explanation:
Triangle WTX has its three angles at W, X and T.
Angle TWX = 90 - p, because side WZ is perpendicular to side WX and angle ZWT = p.
Angle TXW = q.
Angle WTX = 180 - (90 - p) - q = 90 + p - q.
V lies on line XT beyond T, so angle WTV and angle WTX are supplementary: s = 180 - (90 + p - q) = 90 - p + q.
Substitute q = 2p: s = 90 - p + 2p = 90 + p = 124, so p = 34.
Then q = 2p = 68.
Check: s = 90 - 34 + 68 = 124. Geometry check: with p = 34 and q = 68 the two segments meet at about (0.63, 0.93) in a unit square with W at (0,1), so T is inside the square and XT reaches side ZY at about 0.6 of the way from Z.
questions.trap: Solving correctly for p = 34 and stopping there, entering 34 instead of q = 68. Dropping the p term (writing s = 90 + q) gives q = 34 as well.

questions.question: Segment AD has length 44. Point B lies on AD with BD = 19. Point C also lies on AD, and BC = 7. Select all of the values that the length AC could equal.
questions.explanation:
AB = AD - BD = 44 - 19 = 25.
C is 7 units from B along AD, and it can sit on either side of B.
C on the A side of B: AC = AB - BC = 25 - 7 = 18. This is allowed because 7 <= 25.
C on the D side of B: AC = AB + BC = 25 + 7 = 32. This is allowed because 7 <= BD = 19, so C stays on the segment.
A: 12 = BD - BC is not a distance from A. FALSE.
B: 18 is possible. TRUE.
C: 25 would put C at B itself, but BC = 7. FALSE.
D: 32 is possible. TRUE.
E: 37 = 44 - 7 would measure from the wrong end. FALSE.
Answer: B, D.
questions.trap: Placing C on only one side of B, usually between B and D, so only 32 is found (choice D alone), or giving the distance AB itself as the answer (choice C).
